---
title: "Sufficient statistics"
---

The earlier chapter defined a [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) as a function of a parameter with the observed data held fixed. The [exponential-family page](exponential-family.qmd) showed that data enter some likelihoods through a compact sum. Sufficiency states when such a reduction retains all likelihood information about a parameter.

Suppose we observe binary responses $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ under one Bernoulli probability $\pi$. Once we know the number of successes, do the individual orderings of zeroes and ones provide additional information about $\pi$?

## Factor the likelihood

The joint likelihood is

$$
L(\pi)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
\pi^{y_i}(1-\pi)^{1-y_i}.
$$

Collecting exponents gives

$$
L(\pi)
=
\pi^{\sum_i y_i}
(1-\pi)^{n-\sum_i y_i}.
$$

The data affect this likelihood only through $\sum_i y_i$, the number of successes. The order in which the responses occurred does not matter for estimating $\pi$ under this model.

The success count is thus a sufficient statistic for $\pi$.

Sufficiency allows likelihood-irrelevant detail to be omitted from inference about one parameter. The resulting reduction is lossless for inference about $\pi$ under
the stated independent, constant-probability Bernoulli model. It need not be
lossless for another question.

## Compare two ordered response sequences

Consider two sequences of six binary responses:

$$
\mathbf y_A=(1,1,1,0,0,0)
$$

and

$$
\mathbf y_B=(1,0,1,0,1,0).
$$

Both contain three successes and three failures. Under one Bernoulli probability,

$$
L_A(\pi)=\pi^3(1-\pi)^3
$$

and

$$
L_B(\pi)=\pi^3(1-\pi)^3.
$$

At $\pi=.6$, both likelihoods equal

$$
.6^3(.4)^3=.013824.
$$

The model cannot use the clustered successes in sequence A or the alternation in
sequence B to distinguish values of $\pi$. Their sufficient statistic is the
same:

$$
T(\mathbf y_A)=T(\mathbf y_B)=3.
$$

## What sufficiency means

A [**sufficient statistic**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat415/book/export/html/844) $T(\mathbf{Y})$ for parameter $\theta$ is a statistic for which the conditional distribution of the full data given $T(\mathbf{Y})$ does not depend on $\theta$. Informally, after the statistic is known, the remaining details of the sample contain no additional information about that parameter under the assumed model.

The phrase "under the assumed model" is essential. The order of binary responses is irrelevant to an independent Bernoulli model. It may be informative about learning, fatigue, or sequential dependence under another model.

This gives a direct diagnostic question. If the order is scientifically
meaningful, does the fitted model represent the process that could produce an
ordered pattern? Sufficiency says the order is unnecessary for one parameter under one
model. It does not say the order is linguistically meaningless.

## Use the factorization criterion

A statistic $T(\mathbf y)$ is sufficient for $\theta$ if the likelihood can be
written as

$$
L(\theta;\mathbf y)
=h(\mathbf y)g(T(\mathbf y),\theta),
$$

where $h$ does not depend on $\theta$. For the Bernoulli sample,

$$
h(\mathbf y)=1
$$

and

$$
g(T,\pi)=\pi^T(1-\pi)^{n-T}.
$$

All dependence on $\pi$ passes through $T=\sum_i y_i$. This is the
factorization criterion for sufficiency.

## A linguistic example

Suppose a speaker produces a voiced variant on $18$ of $30$ independent tokens
with identical modeled conditions. For a one-probability Bernoulli model, the
pair $(18,30)$ contains the likelihood information about $\pi$.

The log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\pi)
=18\log\pi+12\log(1-\pi).
$$

The individual token order no longer appears. If the number of trials $n$ is
fixed and known, the success count 18 alone supplies the sample-dependent part.

If the trials differ by verb, time phrase, or trial position, collapsing to one count destroys predictor information. Sufficiency is always relative to a parameter and a model.

For instance, suppose the first 15 tokens occur phrase-medially and the last 15
occur phrase-finally. A model with separate position probabilities needs two
success counts, one within each position. The overall count 18 does not say how
successes were divided across the two predictor rows.

The required statistic changed because the parameterization changed. There is
no model-free sufficient summary of a dataset.

## Connection with the exponential family

In a one parameter exponential family, the data enter the likelihood through a statistic such as $\sum_i y_i$. This compact dependence is one reason the family supports a common fitting theory.

It does not license arbitrary aggregation. Regression gives observations different conditional means through their predictors. Two observations with different predictor rows are not interchangeable merely because their responses have the same family.

## Separate inference compression from data storage

A sufficient statistic need not replace the original observations in an
analysis archive. The token-level data may be needed to check independence,
locate coding errors, study later hypotheses, or reconstruct grouped sampling.

The original data should not be deleted merely because one current parameter has
a sufficient statistic. Sufficiency is a likelihood statement. It is not a data-management instruction.

## Calculate the sufficient statistic

```{r}
#| label: calculate-bernoulli-sufficient-statistic
#| echo: true
y_a <- c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
y_b <- c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0)
pi <- .6

c(
  successes_a = sum(y_a),
  successes_b = sum(y_b),
  likelihood_a = prod(pi^y_a * (1 - pi)^(1 - y_a)),
  likelihood_b = prod(pi^y_b * (1 - pi)^(1 - y_b))
)
```

The equal likelihood values verify the hand calculation for this model and
parameter value.

::: {.callout-note title="Identify the model-relative compression"}
1. Why is the number of successes sufficient for one Bernoulli probability?
2. When could response order contain information that this model ignores?
3. Why can regression data not always be reduced to one success count?
4. What sufficient summaries would a two-position Bernoulli model require?
5. Explain why a sufficient statistic does not make the original observations dispensable.
:::
